units.title: Streaming execution and bounded output
units.outcome: Evaluate a query under an explicit engine and resource contract.
units.theory:
Streaming execution processes suitable parts of a query in batches. This can reduce memory pressure and support writing results without materializing every output row as a Python object. It does not mean that every operator uses constant memory or that any dataset will fit any machine. Joins, sorting, distinct operations and high-cardinality group state still require resources determined by the query and data.

The first case compares two engines on the same lazy query and independently checks its numeric total. Engine selection is separated from correctness. The example is intentionally small, so its successful streaming execution is not a claim about an out-of-memory boundary or a production throughput rate. A meaningful capacity study needs controlled dataset size, measured peak memory and a defined machine budget.

A sink can write a result directly to a file, while collect returns a DataFrame to the caller. The second case contrasts a row-preserving transformation with a global reduction. Both can be evaluated through a streaming path, but they produce different shapes and require different state. Output shape and operator semantics should guide the resource plan.
units.syntax: Specify collect(engine="streaming") or collect(engine="in-memory") to make the experiment reproducible against the prepared version. sink_parquet writes the result artifact. Use explicit sorting for equality checks when output order is not otherwise guaranteed. A streamable custom batch function must preserve the result under valid batch partitions; it cannot secretly depend on the full dataset.

worked.title: Compare engines and verify a sink
worked.explanation: A thousand-row fixture is filtered and grouped. The two engine results must agree after the explicit sort, and a written Parquet result must agree with the collected frame. A Python sum independently checks the aggregate.
worked.expected: Both engines and the artifact readback return the same five group totals.

worked.title: Distinguish maps from reductions
worked.explanation: The second case doubles each row and separately computes one global sum. This makes the output-grain difference visible without pretending that either shape alone establishes a memory guarantee.
worked.expected: The map has 20 rows, the reduction 1 row; sum is 190 and doubled sum is 380.

exercises.title: Scale the fixture cautiously
exercises.task: Increase input size within a declared resource budget.
exercises.check: The exact result still matches the independent formula.
exercises.hint: Correctness must survive the scale change.
exercises.answer: Record input size, engine and elapsed time. Do not extrapolate a tiny fixture into a production memory claim.

exercises.title: Change grouping cardinality
exercises.task: Use a nearly unique grouping key.
exercises.check: The result has many more groups.
exercises.hint: Batch processing can still accumulate group state.
exercises.answer: Explain why group cardinality affects memory. Streaming does not erase the state required to retain a result for each key.

exercises.title: Compare collect and sink
exercises.task: Write the same query directly to Parquet.
exercises.check: Readback equals the collected result.
exercises.hint: Inspect the actual output artifact.
exercises.answer: The sink changes how the caller receives output, not the intended values. Keep artifact paths separate from input globs.

exercises.title: Include a global sort
exercises.task: Add an ordered output requirement.
exercises.check: The result obeys the declared order.
exercises.hint: Ordering can require additional coordination and state.
exercises.answer: Measure the query with that requirement included. Removing the sort to obtain a faster number changes the delivered contract.

exercises.title: Reject a false batch claim
exercises.task: Explain why subtracting a full-dataset mean is not independently streamable by arbitrary batches.
exercises.check: The answer identifies dependence on global state.
exercises.hint: Each batch has a different mean.
exercises.answer: A two-pass or accumulated-statistic algorithm can implement the global operation. Centering each batch separately produces a different result.

exercises.title: Report limitations
exercises.task: Write a capacity conclusion supported by this fixture.
exercises.check: The conclusion is bounded to tested sizes and settings.
exercises.hint: A successful process is a lower bound on what worked.
exercises.answer: State the observed inputs, resource configuration and outputs. A maximum supported dataset size requires a separate controlled boundary study.

units.diagnosis: If a supposedly streaming job exhausts memory, inspect operator state, group cardinality, output materialization and accidental conversion into Python objects. If engines disagree, first compare schemas, ordering and floating tolerances before treating the difference as a speed result. Keep engine/version information with the observation.
units.transfer: Evaluate a query under an explicit engine and resource contract. Demonstrate equal logical results, inspect output materialization, and state which scalability questions remain unmeasured. This is the foundation for honest performance engineering.

units.title: Native expressions and the boundary of Python UDFs
units.outcome: Use a Python UDF only with an explicit value, type and batching contract.
units.theory:
A Python user-defined function can express logic that is not available as a native expression. Crossing that boundary can add interpreter overhead, reduce optimization opportunities and introduce hidden state. The right question is whether the extra flexibility is required by the problem and whether its semantics remain valid under the execution strategy.

A return dtype is part of the function contract. It helps the engine reason about downstream operations and avoids relying on accidental inference from an early value. A pure function returns a result from its inputs without depending on mutable external state, time, random global draws or side effects. This is especially important when an engine can evaluate a function in more than one batch or order.

Batch equivalence is stronger than purity alone. Subtracting the mean of each batch is deterministic and pure, but does not equal subtracting the mean of the complete dataset. A streamable declaration must be justified by the operation, not used as a performance switch. The worked counterexample shows two different answers from the same values.
units.syntax: map_elements calls a Python function for values and should declare return_dtype. Compare it with the corresponding native expression before choosing the more expensive interface. The batched counterexample uses ordinary Python arithmetic to expose a semantic issue independently of any query optimizer. A real map_batches adapter additionally needs its output schema and optimization assumptions to be correct.

worked.title: Compare equivalent native and Python functions
worked.explanation: Squaring values has a direct native expression. The Python UDF is included to compare the result and inspect the library warning, not to recommend a slower spelling for ordinary arithmetic. Equality is established on the fixture before discussing cost.
worked.expected: Both implementations return [1,4,9].

worked.title: Show a non-streamable transformation
worked.explanation: The second case centers four values once globally and once within two batches. Both outputs sum to zero, so that aggregate check alone would miss the error. The individual values demonstrate the different transformation.
worked.expected: Global values are [-3,-2,-1,6]; batch-centered values are [-0.5,0.5,-3.5,3.5].

exercises.title: Replace the UDF
exercises.task: Write the square operation using column expressions only.
exercises.check: The values remain [1,4,9].
exercises.hint: Use multiplication on the selected column.
exercises.answer: The native expression keeps semantics visible to the engine. Removing Python callbacks is useful when the native operation actually expresses the same logic.

exercises.title: State a return type
exercises.task: Explain what a UDF returning integers should declare.
exercises.check: It declares the intended integer dtype.
exercises.hint: Schema inference is not a domain specification.
exercises.answer: Choose a dtype that can represent the permitted range, and test overflow or missing output under the intended policy.

exercises.title: Change batch boundaries
exercises.task: Center [1,2,3,10] in a different partition.
exercises.check: The batchwise answer changes while the global answer does not.
exercises.hint: Try three values in the first batch.
exercises.answer: The batch mean depends on the partition. That is why a partition-independent declaration would be false for this implementation.

exercises.title: Find a weak check
exercises.task: Explain why a zero-sum check misses the centering defect.
exercises.check: Both incorrect and correct outputs can sum to zero.
exercises.hint: Check identified intermediate values.
exercises.answer: Use an independent row-level oracle or a property that distinguishes the intended operation. A convenient invariant may be necessary but insufficient.

exercises.title: Introduce hidden state
exercises.task: Describe the risk of incrementing a global counter inside a UDF.
exercises.check: Output can depend on evaluation order or batching.
exercises.hint: The engine controls evaluation strategy.
exercises.answer: Keep counters outside the value transformation for diagnostics, or compute counts with explicit reductions. Do not use callback side effects as record identity.

exercises.title: Design a valid two-pass method
exercises.task: Explain how to perform global centering in bounded stages.
exercises.check: First obtain the global mean, then subtract that fixed value.
exercises.hint: Separate estimation from application.
exercises.answer: The first stage aggregates sufficient information. The second uses a constant derived from that declared population. Keep both stages within the correct train/time boundary.

units.diagnosis: An inefficient-map warning is useful evidence that a native operation may exist. It is not proof that every UDF is wrong. A changed answer under batching is more serious: inspect hidden state, global reductions and schema promises. Do not disable validation flags solely to make a query execute.
units.transfer: Use a Python UDF only with an explicit value, type and batching contract. Demonstrate equivalence to a trusted result on contrasting fixtures and identify which optimization claims are justified. Preserve a native implementation whenever it is clearer and semantically equivalent.

units.title: Performance measurements with correctness controls
units.outcome: Produce a reviewable performance comparison with a correctness oracle.
units.theory:
A timing number becomes useful only when the measured work is defined. Query construction, schema discovery, file I/O, computation, conversion to Python objects and serialization can contribute different costs. A benchmark that times only construction of a lazy object has not measured execution. A warm repeated query over an in-memory frame is also different from a cold read of a newly opened dataset.

The first case collects the query on every repetition and checks its answer. It reports a median across a small number of observations rather than declaring the smallest observed value to be a stable property. The fixture is deliberately modest so it can run inside the classroom budget. No assertion says that one engine must beat another, because tiny timings are noisy and hardware dependent.

Performance comparisons must preserve the output contract. An unordered result can be compared as a set or multiset when order is irrelevant; an ordered consumer needs the sorting cost included. The second case distinguishes bag equality from sequence equality. This prevents a supposed optimization from silently removing an ordering requirement.
units.syntax: perf_counter measures elapsed time around the actual collect call. Record the engine and the number of repetitions. estimated_size describes the frame's buffer estimate, not the whole process peak or every temporary allocation. Sort only when that is part of the intended comparison, and account for its cost explicitly.

worked.title: Measure completed work with an independent answer
worked.explanation: The query filters twenty thousand synthetic values and sums them. A Python expression computes the expected answer independently. Every measured execution must match it, and the report includes row count and an estimate of input buffer size.
worked.expected: All five results match the exact sum; timings are nonnegative and the median is reported without a speed claim.

worked.title: Separate sequence from content
worked.explanation: The second case compares a shuffled frame with a sorted one. Sorting the shuffled result establishes the same identified content, while the unsorted sequence may differ. The original frame also remains unchanged.
worked.expected: The sorted values are [1,2,3]; bag equality holds after sorting.

exercises.title: Include file I/O
exercises.task: Move fixture creation outside timing and measure a fresh file scan separately.
exercises.check: The report identifies what was included.
exercises.hint: Setup and timed work are different phases.
exercises.answer: Do not count fixture generation as query execution unless that is the workflow under evaluation. Record the filesystem and cache conditions where relevant.

exercises.title: Vary scale
exercises.task: Repeat at two declared input sizes.
exercises.check: Answers remain correct at both sizes.
exercises.hint: Keep the data-generation rule stable.
exercises.answer: A scaling observation requires comparable work and resource settings. Two points do not establish a universal complexity curve or an operational capacity limit.

exercises.title: Report variability
exercises.task: Keep every timing rather than only the fastest.
exercises.check: The raw repetitions and a summary are available.
exercises.hint: A median does not replace raw observations.
exercises.answer: Report the distribution and context. Large variability may come from scheduling, I/O caches, compilation or background activity.

exercises.title: Avoid a false memory claim
exercises.task: Explain why estimated_size is not process peak memory.
exercises.check: The answer names temporary and runtime overhead.
exercises.hint: Buffer size is one component.
exercises.answer: Use an appropriate process-level measurement for a peak claim, and specify whether shared buffers and child processes are counted.

exercises.title: Preserve sorting cost
exercises.task: Compare two queries whose consumers require ordered rows.
exercises.check: Both timings include the required order.
exercises.hint: Equivalent values alone are insufficient.
exercises.answer: Removing sort changes the delivered contract. If order is unnecessary, document that decision and compare multiset equality instead.

exercises.title: Write a bounded conclusion
exercises.task: Summarize what the benchmark demonstrates.
exercises.check: It names data size, engine, version and measurement scope.
exercises.hint: Do not generalize from one machine.
exercises.answer: State the measured result and uncertainty. A claim about production throughput needs representative data, concurrency, failure behavior and service-level requirements.

units.diagnosis: Near-zero timings may indicate that execution was omitted. Very different answers indicate a correctness problem before they indicate a performance win. Avoid benchmark assertions such as always faster, and keep expensive experiments within declared limits. A slow first run may include compilation or initialization that later runs do not repeat.
units.transfer: Produce a reviewable performance comparison with a correctness oracle. State the measured operation, data size, ordering requirement, cache regime and resource environment, and retain all repetitions. Use the result to choose the next experiment rather than treating a microbenchmark as a production guarantee.

units.title: A validated event-to-feature publication
units.outcome: Publish a feature artifact with explicit derivation and consumption contracts.
units.theory:
The final case combines several contracts rather than introducing another table method. Raw events arrive with identifiers, customer keys, textual amounts and event times. One event is repeated and another has an invalid amount. A reliable pipeline should account for both before publishing a customer-level feature table. A final total alone cannot explain which records were rejected or duplicated.

The deduplication in this fixture is justified because the repeated event has identical content. Conflicting versions of one event would require a reviewed ordering or conflict policy; unique(subset=...) must not arbitrarily choose a winner in that situation. The accepted rows then produce one result per customer, with an event count beside the amount total. This makes the change from event grain to customer grain explicit.

The second case writes a typed artifact and a receipt containing its hash, schema, row count and grain. A cryptographic hash establishes byte identity, not correctness or authenticity by itself. Readback checks the published content, while the earlier row accounting checks how it was derived. In a durable system, publication would also need ownership, atomicity, lineage and a retention policy.
units.syntax: Parse into a new field, isolate invalid rows, apply the declared duplicate rule and only then aggregate. Use a stable sort before publishing an ordered result. write_parquet creates the typed output; hashlib.sha256 records its exact bytes; a JSON receipt makes the contract inspectable. A hash can legitimately change when a library writes an equivalent Parquet encoding, so distinguish byte identity from logical equality.

worked.title: Account for every event
worked.explanation: The five source rows become three accepted unique events, one malformed event and one duplicate copy. Customer totals are derived only from accepted events. The count equation makes it impossible to describe this as simply cleaning away inconvenient rows.
worked.expected: Customer 10 has total 12 from 2 events; customer 20 has total 9 from 1 event; one malformed and one duplicate row are recorded.

worked.title: Publish and inspect a typed artifact
worked.explanation: The second case writes the feature table and a receipt, then reads both back. It verifies the file hash and logical contents independently. This is a local publication mechanism, not a claim that a distributed transactional service has been deployed.
worked.expected: Readback preserves two unique customers, the schema and exact artifact hash.

exercises.title: Introduce conflicting duplicates
exercises.task: Change one repeated event amount while keeping its id.
exercises.check: The pipeline explicitly rejects or resolves the conflict under a stated rule.
exercises.hint: Identical retries differ from conflicting versions.
exercises.answer: Compare content per event_id before selecting a record. A version timestamp or authority rule must be justified; arbitrary first/last selection is not a data contract.

exercises.title: Reconcile the source
exercises.task: Write the complete row-accounting equation.
exercises.check: 5 source rows = 3 accepted unique + 1 invalid + 1 duplicate.
exercises.hint: Keep categories mutually exclusive.
exercises.answer: Apply classification in a documented order and verify identifiers in each outcome. Ambiguous overlap makes reported quality counts unreliable.

exercises.title: Check final grain
exercises.task: Assert one output row per customer.
exercises.check: Unique customer count equals output height.
exercises.hint: An aggregate should have a declared key.
exercises.answer: Validate the final key and compare additive totals with accepted events. This checks both shape and quantity preservation.

exercises.title: Tamper with an artifact
exercises.task: Change the output bytes after writing its receipt.
exercises.check: The hash check detects the difference.
exercises.hint: A stored hash describes particular bytes.
exercises.answer: Recompute and compare before consuming the artifact. A new matching hash written by the same attacker would need an authenticity boundary that this local example does not provide.

exercises.title: Distinguish two equalities
exercises.task: Explain byte identity versus logical table equality.
exercises.check: The explanation allows equivalent encodings with different hashes.
exercises.hint: Parquet metadata and encoding choices can differ.
exercises.answer: Use hashes for exact artifacts and schema/value checks for a logical transformation contract. Record the writer version when byte reproducibility matters.

exercises.title: Design the next boundary
exercises.task: Specify what a model-training consumer must verify.
exercises.check: It includes schema, grain, availability, missingness and data identity.
exercises.hint: A readable file is not necessarily suitable training input.
exercises.answer: The consumer should validate its expected version and reject incompatible or temporally invalid features. The ML engineering path carries these checks into training and serving.

units.diagnosis: If counts do not reconcile, inspect classification order and duplicate semantics. If an output hash changes, determine whether bytes changed, the receipt is stale or a different encoding was produced. If a model receives future information, correct the temporal contract before improving model hyperparameters. Preserve rejected evidence and the publication decision.
units.transfer: Publish a feature artifact with explicit derivation and consumption contracts. Extend the case with a conflicting duplicate and a late-known event, then document why publication is accepted or blocked. Use this result as a foundation for the analytics-engineering and ML-engineering paths rather than assuming a clean-looking table is a complete data product.
